request.system:
You assist an automated astronomer who infers how a body moves from angles-only sky observations (ecliptic longitude/latitude seen from an observer whose orbit is known). Jan, the fitting engine, fits candidate model families by least squares and compares them by Bayesian evidence. You see numerical summaries of the current best fit and its residuals, and you propose the next candidates to fit.

A candidate is either a registered family (by exact name) or a new central force law: the radial acceleration f(r) in AU/day^2 (negative = attractive) as an expression in r (heliocentric distance, AU), GM (the Sun's, 2.959e-4 AU^3/day^2, fixed) and parameters you declare with bounds and an initial value. Allowed in expressions: numbers, + - * / **, parentheses, exp, log, sqrt, tanh, pi, r, GM and your parameter names (lowercase, letters/digits/underscore). Prefer the simplest law that explains the residual structure; a new parameter must buy a clear improvement. Reply "stop": true when the residuals are consistent with noise or further candidates are unlikely to help.

parsed.analysis:
The current fits are effectively failing, not just imperfect. The fitted noise sigma is about 45 deg and the residual RMS is about 85 deg, so the model is barely tracking the body.

The best power law sits at an essentially Newtonian strength: C*r^-2.16 is about GM/r^2 at 3 AU. Under that strength a body at r≈3.1 AU should have a period near 1990 days.

The half-span ellipse fits disagree with that. They give periods of 600–860 days, which implies an effective attraction of order 5–10 GM at about 3 AU. A plausible explanation is that every integrated fit has been trapped in the wrong basin for the mean motion.

The ellipse fits also show a prograde apsidal advance of about 17 deg per orbit. For a pure power law, apsidal angle π/sqrt(3-n) gives n≈2.09.

I propose re-parameterised laws whose strength is normalised at 3 AU and whose initial values sit in the high-strength basin.

proposals.rationale: The 600–860 d periods at r≈3.1 AU imply an attraction several times solar. A one-parameter scaled Newton law started near k≈7 tests whether the previous fits were stuck in a wrong mean-motion basin.
Normalising at 3 AU decorrelates strength from exponent. The initial n=2.09 matches the ~17 deg/orbit prograde apsidal advance seen in the half-span ellipse fits.

This is an alternative way to produce the observed precession on top of a strong central attraction. An inverse-cube term with eps/r≈0.03–0.1 near 3 AU would give an apsidal advance of order 10–20 deg per orbit.
